questions.answer: The common symptoms of diabetes include increased urination [1], feeling very thirsty [1], feeling very hungry [1], blurred vision [1], fatigue [1], sores that do not heal [1], frequent infections such as yeast infections, urinary tract infections, or skin infections [1]. For type 2 diabetes, additional symptoms may include pain, numbness, or tingling in the feet or hands, sexual problems, chest pain, and vision loss [2]. Type 1 diabetes can also cause unexplained weight loss [3], feeling very thirsty [4], having to urinate more often [4], eating more but losing weight [4], and experiencing diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) symptoms such as feeling very tired, having trouble breathing, having fruity-smelling breath, fainting from dehydration, or abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting [4]. - feeling very tired [1, 2]
- having trouble breathing [1, 2]
- having fruity-smelling breath [1, 2]
- fainting from dehydration [1, 2]

These symptoms align with the information provided in passages [1] and [2]. Passage [3] also mentions these signs but does not provide additional specific details. The main risk factors for type 2 diabetes include being overweight or obese [1], age 35 or older [2], having a family history of diabetes [2], belonging to certain racial or ethnic groups such as African American, American Indian, Asian American, Hispanic/Latino, or Pacific Islander [2], not being physically active due to physical limitations, sedentary lifestyle, or long periods of sitting at work [2], having prediabetes [2], and a history of gestational diabetes or giving birth to a baby weighing 9 pounds or more [2]. Additionally, waist circumference is another risk factor for type 2 diabetes; men have a higher risk if their waist circumference exceeds 40 inches, while women not pregnant have a higher risk if it exceeds 35 inches [5]. Insufficient information on low birth weight and gestational diabetes in children/teens from parents with gestational diabetes is provided.
[1] states that losing 5 to 7 percent of your starting weight can help prevent or delay type 2 diabetes. For a person weighing 200 pounds, this would be about 10 to 14 pounds [1].

If you have prediabetes, you can lower your chance of developing type 2 diabetes by losing weight if needed, becoming more physically active, and following a reduced-calorie eating plan [1, 2]. You should also get tested for diabetes 6 to 12 weeks after your baby is born if you had gestational diabetes during pregnancy. If your blood glucose remains high, you may have type 2 diabetes; otherwise, you should be tested every 3 years. Additionally, breastfeeding can help you return to a healthy weight and burn calories [5]. For more support, consider joining a National Diabetes Prevention Program lifestyle change program [2].
The A1C test measures your average blood glucose level over the last 3 months [1].

The diabetes ABCs include the A1C test (a measure of average blood glucose over 3 months) [2], managing blood pressure with a goal below 130/80 mm Hg [3], cholesterol levels, and stopping smoking [5]. These components help manage your health to prevent complications from diabetes. [1]

[1] recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity each week to help manage blood glucose levels, among other benefits [1]. Moderate-intensity activities include brisk walking. Muscle-strengthening exercises should be done two days a week for additional health benefits.

Waist circumference is important for diabetes risk because it's an indirect measurement of abdominal fat, which is a risk factor for both diabetes and heart disease [1]. Having a large waist circumference indicates higher levels of visceral fat around the abdomen, contributing to insulin resistance and increasing the likelihood of developing type 2 diabetes [1].

Type 1 diabetes develops when the body's immune system destroys the cells in the pancreas that make insulin [1]. This destruction of beta cells leads to insufficient insulin production, which is necessary for blood glucose to enter the body’s cells and provide energy. Without enough insulin, glucose builds up in the bloodstream, causing high levels of sugar (glucose) in the blood, a condition known as hyperglycemia. This can result in symptoms such as feeling very tired, having trouble breathing, fruity-smelling breath, fainting from dehydration, or abdominal pain [3]. Insufficient insulin also causes fat to be used for energy instead, leading to high levels of ketones which can cause DKA if not treated promptly [1]. The exact cause of the immune system's destruction of beta cells in type 1 diabetes is not fully understood; however, it involves a combination of genetic and environmental factors [2].

Type 2 diabetes develops when your pancreas doesn’t produce enough insulin, and your body has trouble using insulin [1]. Insulin resistance occurs when the cells in your muscles, fat, and liver don't respond well to insulin [1]. When there isn't enough insulin to balance blood glucose levels, they begin to rise [1]. Type 2 diabetes is often preventable due to factors such as being overweight, not getting enough exercise, or having a family history of the disease [4]. Other risk factors include age, race, and exposure to secondhand smoke [1-2]. Insufficient context

Some medicines can raise the risk of diabetes [1]. Medicines like antipsychotics, antiseizure medicines, beta-blockers, diuretics, glucocorticoids, immunosuppressants, niacin, statins, metformin, sulfonylureas, and sodium-glucose co-transporters type 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors can affect the risk [1, 3]. Insulin injections are also used for diabetes management. Managing health conditions and discussing medications with a doctor is important to reduce the risk of developing diabetes [5].

The risk factors for high blood pressure include:
- Unhealthy lifestyle habits that can be changed (e.g., eating unhealthy foods often) [5]
- Age-related changes in the body [3]
- Other medical conditions such as kidney disease and thyroid problems [4]
- Social and economic factors like income, education level, job type, and stressors at work [2]
- Genetics and family history that cannot be changed [1]

To lower high blood pressure, lifestyle changes include eating more vegetables and fruits [1], sitting less [1], being physically active like walking or swimming for at least 150 minutes per week [1], losing weight if overweight or obese [1], taking medicines as prescribed by your health care professional [1], and keeping appointments with your healthcare provider [1]. Additionally, avoid alcohol, get regular physical activity, aim for a healthy weight, quit smoking, control cholesterol and blood sugar levels, manage stress, and ensure enough good-quality sleep [5].
Hypertension is diagnosed when the systolic blood pressure readings on both days is ≥140 mmHg and/or the diastolic blood pressure readings on both days is ≥90 mmHg [1].

Silent heart attacks are different from typical heart attacks where chest pain is the main symptom [2]. They can be hard to detect, especially if they only cause minor discomfort or none at all.

According to the World Health Organization (WHO), lifestyle changes are the best way to prevent or delay the onset of type 2 diabetes [2]. To help prevent type 2 diabetes, people should:

- Reach and keep a health body weight
- Stay physically active with at least 150 minutes of moderate exercise each week
- Eat a healthy diet and avoid sugar and saturated fat
- Not smoke tobacco

These lifestyle changes include losing weight by aiming for a modest reduction in your starting weight (e.g., 5 to 7% or about 10 to 14 pounds if you weigh 200 pounds) [3], being physically active with at least 30 minutes of exercise most days, and eating healthy foods while reducing portion sizes and fat intake. Additionally, quitting smoking can also help prevent type 2 diabetes [2].
